messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Shouting: Shouting, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Vignette:
Nadia is a 38-year-old married Middle Eastern American woman who works as a housekeeper in a downtown hotel. When she describes the assault, she does so in fragments, with certain moments landing in sharp, painful detail while the larger sequence still feels torn away from her. She remembers being cornered and overpowered by a man who forced her compliance while shouting at her. The sound of his voice is one of the pieces that has stayed with unnatural clarity. She can recall the pressure on her body and the specific places where she was hurt, and when the memory comes back she feels pain again in those same areas, as if her body is repeating what happened before her mind can fully make sense of it. Other parts of the event are simply absent to her. She knows something happened between one clear image and the next, but she cannot access it, and this missing middle unsettles her. She says it is like holding torn pages from a story she did not survive in one piece.

In the weeks after the assault, Nadia found that reminders did not arrive as ordinary memories. They hit as sudden returns of sensation and alarm. If she heard shouting, even from far away, her whole body reacted before she could tell herself she was somewhere else. What frightened her most was not only the noise itself but what it stood for: a person forcing their will onto her, the moment when she had no control over what was being done to her. She had come to dread any situation in which someone might press her, corner her, or tell her she had no choice. Even small moments could take on that feeling. If a supervisor at the hotel sharply instructed her to redo a room immediately, she could feel panic rising, not because the task was difficult but because being ordered in a harsh tone made her feel trapped. At times she would freeze, lose the thread of what she was doing, and stand in the supply closet trying to remember which cart belonged to her or which room she had just finished.

Her work environment exposes her to reminders she cannot reliably avoid. Part of her job involves cleaning rooms after guests leave, and on some mornings she passes through floors where families are checking out after medical visits or where she sees women who appear frail, frightened, or injured. Reminders of victims affect her strongly. A glimpse of a woman crying in the hallway, or of someone speaking softly to an obviously shaken guest, can pull her into the same internal state she associates with the assault. She does not describe this as empathy alone. It is as if the sight tells her instantly that terrible things happen to defenseless people and can happen again. She then becomes intensely alert to everything around her.

That alertness now follows her almost constantly. Nadia scans her surroundings for danger in ways that leave her exhausted. In hotel corridors she notices who is near the stairwell, whose footsteps pause behind her, whether a voice around the corner sounds angry. At home she listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering. If the building creaks at night or a neighbor comes in late, she is immediately awake, listening hard, trying to identify whether the sound means an intruder is inside. Her husband has noticed that she checks the locks repeatedly and goes still whenever there is noise in the hallway. She is not able to settle easily once she starts listening. Her attention narrows to possible signs of danger, and ordinary tasks become difficult. She loses focus while folding laundry, misses ingredients while cooking, and has to restart chores because her concentration slips away.

What troubles Nadia deeply is the broken quality of the memory itself. She is certain that some moments are exact: the shouting, the force used against her, the pain in her body. Yet so much else is missing that she does not feel she possesses a full account of what happened. She returns again and again to the blank spaces, trying to understand them, and is distressed that she cannot. The gaps make her feel vulnerable in a particular way, as though not knowing every part leaves her unprotected.

Over months, these patterns have narrowed her life. At work she tries to keep to quieter floors and avoid situations where she might be alone near loud guests or maintenance staff arguing in the hall. At home she is tense when anyone raises their voice, even during ordinary family frustration. She has become more guarded with her husband, not because she does not trust him, but because what she cannot bear is the feeling of being pushed or overruled. She finally sought help after realizing how much of each day was organized around listening, watching, and bracing. She said she is tired of feeling as though danger is about to come through every doorway. At the same time, she is afraid that speaking in detail will bring back the pain in her body and the parts of the assault that remain sharply alive, while the missing parts may never come back at all.
